148.title: The fast God chooses (Isaiah 58:6–7)
148.hook: loosen the bands, share your bread, don't hide from your own flesh
148.howItsDone: Many Christians pair fasting with giving, setting aside the money they would have spent on food during Lent or on fast days and giving it to the poor, often through church collections or food banks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: from the ancient Didache's Wednesdays and Fridays to Orthodox and Catholic Lent and Protestants fasting for a cause. Your line was make space.

Everything done right. The meals skipped. The rough clothes on. The head bowed all day. The whole routine, carefully kept, and nothing happens. So the complaint goes up, a little hurt: we fasted, God, and you didn't even notice. The prophet Isaiah hears it from his people, and God's answer through him is blunt. You fast, and on the same day you're squeezing your workers. You fast, and you're picking fights. Then comes a question that turns fasting inside out.
screen: `WE FASTED. YOU DIDN'T NOTICE.` → `SAME DAY, SQUEEZING YOUR WORKERS.` → `A QUESTION THAT TURNS IT INSIDE OUT.`

segments.voice: In Isaiah fifty-eight, the people ask, in the King James Bible: "Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not?" God answers with a different kind of fast. "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?" Fasting was about what you don't eat. Here, it's about who else gets to eat: your empty plate is supposed to become someone else's full one. Isaiah isn't throwing out fasting; he's saying a fast that leaves the hungry hungry has missed the point. And that last line, hide not thyself from thine own flesh: your own flesh means your own people, your family, your neighbor, the human being in front of you. Don't look away. Don't cross the street. And a promise: "Then shall thy light break forth as the morning." Jews read this chapter aloud on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, right in the middle of the fast. Christians lean on it too: in the custom of giving to the poor what you'd have spent on food during Lent, and in movements for justice that quoted Isaiah to the powerful. The prophet asks every fast the same question: who got fed?

segments.voice: Think of what you'll spend on yourself today that you could skip, a coffee out, a lunch, a delivery fee, a small treat, and put a number on it. Picture where that money could go instead, a food bank, a neighbor who's short this month, the person asking for change outside the store, and, without guilt, let Isaiah's picture sit with you: your empty plate becoming someone's full one. If you pray, pray for someone who is hungry today.
Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, when Jews read this chapter aloud, right in the middle of the fast that feeds the hungry.
Your line: fast to feed. An empty plate can fill another. One hundred forty-eight days now.

149.title: One thing I know (John 9:25)
149.hook: a healed blind man can't win the argument, but he knows he was blind and now sees
149.carry: I was blind, now I see
149.howItsDone: In many churches, people share their testimony, a short account of what they believe God has done in their lives, in services, small groups or baptisms; others keep it as a private record of answered prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Isaiah's fast that feeds the hungry, read on Yom Kippur. Your line was fast to feed.

Ever argued with someone much cleverer than you? They have the vocabulary, the confidence, an answer for every point. You walk away thinking: I couldn't win that, but I still know what I know. That's where a man in the Gospel of John ends up. Born blind, he begged by the road. Jesus spat on the ground, made mud, put it on his eyes and told him to go wash in the pool of Siloam. He went, washed, and came back seeing. That should be the happy ending. Instead, an interrogation begins.
screen: `BORN BLIND, BEGGING BY THE ROAD.` → `MUD, A POOL, AND SIGHT.` → `THEN THE INTERROGATION.`

segments.voice: Testimony is what a witness says about what they've seen. In John chapter nine, almost nobody is glad. The neighbors argue about whether it's even the same man; some say he just looks like him, and he keeps saying: I am he. Then religious leaders question him. It was the Sabbath, so some say the healer can't be from God, while others ask how a sinner could do such signs. They're divided. They call in his parents, who are afraid and say: he's of age, ask him. They call him back and press him: we know this man is a sinner. His answer, in the King James Bible: "Whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see." He doesn't win the theology, and doesn't claim to. He just tells what happened. The Greek word is martyria, and a witness is a martys, the root of our word martyr. At first it simply meant witness; later, as Christians died for what they testified, it came to mean one who dies for their faith. He gets bolder under pressure and is put out. Then Jesus finds him, and he goes from calling Jesus a man, to a prophet, to worshipping him. John tells it as a story about sight: the one who was blind sees more and more. Much later, a former slave-ship captain named John Newton borrowed his words for a hymn: "I once was lost, but now am found, Was blind, but now I see." A testimony doesn't need to be clever. It just needs to be true.
screen: `THE NEIGHBORS ARGUE: IS IT HIM?` · `HE CAN'T WIN THE THEOLOGY.` · `MARTYRIA — WHAT A WITNESS SAYS.` · `WAS BLIND, BUT NOW I SEE.` · then, large: `ONE THING I KNOW.`

segments.voice: Let the questions about God or life you can't answer, the arguments you'd lose, be there. Then look for one thing you know, not a doctrine but something that happened to you: a moment you were helped, a time you were forgiven, a night you somehow got through, a change you can't fully explain. If you pray, give thanks for it; if you don't, just hold it.
Testimony. What a witness says: not the argument, just what happened. In Greek, martyria, the root of martyr.
Your line: I was blind, now I see. See you on day one hundred fifty.

150.title: Your story in three sentences
150.hook: many churches invite people to tell what God has done; it can be very small
150.howItsDone: Many churches invite members to share a short testimony at baptisms, small groups or services; Quakers may speak out of silence in meeting, and Catholic and Orthodox parishes often share stories at retreats and in the lives of the saints.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a healed man who couldn't win the argument, and your line: I was blind, now I see. This week: fellowship, small groups, carrying burdens, church hurt, quiet, stillness, fasting and one thing I know.
screen: `I WAS BLIND, NOW I SEE.` → `A WEEK OF TOGETHER AND ALONE.`

segments.voice: A man has been living among the tombs. People had chained him, and he broke the chains. He cut himself with stones and cried out day and night. Then Jesus comes to his side of the lake, and by the end the man is sitting there, clothed, calm, in his right mind. As Jesus gets back in the boat, the man begs to come with him. Of course he does. And Jesus says no. Not because he's unwanted. Because he has a job: go home, and tell. No training, no script, no theology course.
screen: `A MAN AMONG THE TOMBS.` → `CLOTHED, AND IN HIS RIGHT MIND.` → `GO HOME, AND TELL THEM.`

segments.voice: In Mark five, in the King James Bible: "Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee." Two things to tell: what was done, and the compassion behind it. A psalm agrees: "Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul." Early Methodists held love feasts, simple meals of bread and water where people stood and told what God was doing in their lives. Baptist and Pentecostal churches often make room for testimony, especially at baptisms. Quakers sit in silence until someone is moved to speak. Catholics and Orthodox tell the stories of the saints, and many parishes invite people to share their own at retreats. People who've heard a lot of testimonies say the best ones are small and plain. Not a sermon. Not a before-and-after movie. Just what happened. Many teachers suggest three parts: where I was, what happened, where I am now. Three sentences. It doesn't need to be dramatic. I was lonely at college; a friend brought me to a Bible study; I'm still not sure about everything, but I'm not lonely anymore. That counts. So does: I was angry for years; one night I prayed the Lord's Prayer and meant the forgive part; I'm still working on it. No preaching, no telling anyone what to believe. Just your story, told honestly, the way the man from the tombs told his.
screen: `GO HOME AND TELL THY FRIENDS.` · `LOVE FEASTS, BAPTISMS, SILENCE.` · `WHERE I WAS, WHAT HAPPENED, NOW.` · `SMALL, PLAIN, NO PREACHING.` · then, large: `WHAT HE HATH DONE FOR MY SOUL.`

segments.voice: Take the one thing you know from yesterday and give it those three parts, each sentence plain, with no big words and no conclusion. If your story is about God, say so; if it's about a friend, a book or a hard night, that's fine too. Say the three sentences quietly to yourself, and if you pray, offer them as thanks.
Testimony, a small, honest telling of where I was, what happened, and where I am now, the way the man from the tombs told his.
Your line: your story counts. Even the small ones. A hundred and fifty days, and counting.

151.title: Signs you can touch
151.hook: Catholics and Orthodox count seven sacraments; most Protestants two ordinances; Quakers keep them inwardly
151.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians celebrate seven sacraments across life, from baptism to anointing of the sick; most Protestant churches celebrate baptism and the Lord's Supper; Quakers and the Salvation Army keep no outward sacraments.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your story in three sentences, a testimony. Your line was your story counts. Now a new week, and the last of this camp: the sacraments, briefly.
screen: `YOUR STORY COUNTS.` → `A NEW WEEK: THE SACRAMENTS.`

segments.voice: A ring slid onto a finger. A hand on a shoulder at a funeral. A handshake that closes a deal. A hug at the airport. None of them needs a word. People are bodies, and the deepest things they mean, they tend to say with hands, with objects, with water and bread and touch. Christianity is full of this. Water poured over a baby's head. Bread broken and shared. Oil smoothed on a sick person's forehead. Hands laid on someone being sent out. For many Christians these are not just symbols. They're where God meets people, through ordinary stuff. And the churches count them differently.
screen: `A RING, A HANDSHAKE, A HUG.` → `WATER, BREAD, OIL, HANDS.` → `WHERE GOD MEETS PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Sacrament comes from the Latin sacramentum, and before the church used it, it meant a soldier's oath of loyalty, something sacred that binds you. Early Latin Christians used it to translate a Greek word, mysterion, mystery; Orthodox Christians still call the sacraments the holy mysteries. A classic definition, from the Anglican Book of Common Prayer: a sacrament is "an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace." Outward and visible: water, bread, wine, oil. Inward and spiritual: what God gives through them. The churches count differently. Catholics count seven, and Orthodox Christians usually name the same seven: baptism; confirmation, which Orthodox call chrismation; the Eucharist; confession; anointing of the sick; marriage; and ordination. Most Protestant churches name two, baptism and the Lord's Supper, because Jesus commanded those two directly. Many Baptists and others prefer the word ordinance: something ordered by Christ, done in obedience and remembrance. Anglicans and Lutherans hold the two as sacraments and treat the others as sacred rites. A few, like Quakers and the Salvation Army, keep no outward sacraments at all. Not because they don't care, but because they believe the reality should be lived inwardly and in every ordinary moment, not in a few set rites. Churches disagree about this in earnest, and each has reasons. What they share is the conviction that God isn't only up in the clouds. God comes close through water on skin, bread in a hand, a word spoken over you. Grace, for many Christians, comes wrapped in the most ordinary things.
screen: `SACRAMENTUM — A SACRED OATH.` · `OUTWARD SIGN, INWARD GRACE.` · `SEVEN, TWO, OR NONE OUTWARDLY.` · `GOD COMES CLOSE THROUGH ORDINARY THINGS.` · then, large: `AN OUTWARD AND VISIBLE SIGN.`

segments.voice: Think of the ordinary things you'll touch today: water from the tap or in a glass, bread or whatever your bread is, lotion or oil on your hands, the hand of someone you love. Pick one and imagine it carrying more than it seems to: care, welcome, life. If you pray, give thanks for it; if you don't, just let it be more than ordinary for a minute.
Sacrament. From the Latin for a sacred oath. An outward sign of inward grace: water, bread, oil, hands.
Your line: grace comes in ordinary things. Water, bread, oil, hands. That's day one hundred fifty-one.

152.title: Baptism, two ways
152.hook: many churches baptize infants into the family; Baptists and others baptize believers who choose
152.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and Presbyterian churches baptize infants with water in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit; Baptist, Pentecostal and many other churches baptize believers who ask for it, usually by full immersion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sacrament, an outward sign of inward grace, counted seven, two or none. Your line was grace comes in ordinary things.

Two scenes, one Sunday. In the first, a baby in a long white gown is held over a stone font. She has no idea what's happening, and may be yelling about it. A priest pours water over her head three times and says her name aloud, and the whole congregation promises to help raise her. In the second, a twenty-five-year-old in a T-shirt wades into a pool at the front of a church, or into a river. He tells, in a few sentences, why he's there. The pastor lowers him all the way under and brings him back up, dripping, to cheering. Both churches call it the same thing.
screen: `A BABY OVER A STONE FONT.` → `A MAN WADES INTO THE RIVER.` → `THE SAME WORD FOR BOTH.`

segments.voice: Baptism, from the Greek baptizō: to dip, to plunge, to immerse. Nearly every Christian tradition baptizes, pointing to Jesus's own command at the end of Matthew's gospel, in the King James Bible: "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Almost all churches baptize with water, in that threefold name, and for most it happens once. The big difference is when. Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and Presbyterians baptize infants. Grace comes first, they say, before we can earn it or even understand it. A baby is brought into God's family the way she's born into her own. They point to Acts, where whole households were baptized together. Orthodox Christians immerse the baby three times, then give chrismation and communion right away. Baptists, Pentecostals and many other churches baptize believers, people old enough to choose. In the New Testament, they say, people heard, believed and then were baptized. They point to an Ethiopian official in Acts who sees water by the road and asks: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?" For them, baptism is a public yes, and full immersion pictures dying and rising with Christ. Each side has its texts and reasons, and some families include both. In many traditions, baptism is also when your name is spoken over you; that's why some still call a first name a Christian name.
screen: `BAPTIZŌ — TO DIP, TO IMMERSE.` · `IN THE NAME OF FATHER, SON AND SPIRIT.` · `INFANTS: GRACE COMES FIRST.` · `BELIEVERS: A PUBLIC YES.` · then, large: `WHAT DOTH HINDER ME TO BE BAPTIZED?`

segments.voice: Say your own first name, quietly, and notice that someone gave it to you: spoken over water in a church, written on a form in a hospital, or a name you've since chosen for yourself. If you were baptized, you might remember that day or who was there. If you pray, give thanks for whoever named you; if you don't, just hold your name as a gift.
Baptism. From the Greek for dipping or immersing. Water and a name, for infants in many churches and for believers in others.
Your line: you were named. Whatever its story, it's a gift. Day one hundred fifty-two, done.

153.title: The table, many views
153.hook: Mass, Divine Liturgy, Lord's Supper: Catholics and Orthodox say Christ is truly present; many Protestants say spiritually, or by remembrance
153.howItsDone: Christians share the Eucharist, also called Mass, the Divine Liturgy, the Lord's Supper or Holy Communion, with bread and wine or grape juice; Catholic and Orthodox churches celebrate it at least every Sunday, while some Protestant churches share it monthly or quarterly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: baptism, water and a name, for infants in many churches and for choosing believers in others. Your line was you were named.

This Sunday, in churches of every kind, the same meal will be shared in very different ways. In a Catholic cathedral, a priest lifts a round white host while a bell rings. In an Orthodox church, a spoon of bread soaked in wine goes onto a child's tongue. In a Baptist church, trays of tiny cups of grape juice pass down the pews. In a Lutheran church, people kneel at a rail. Mass, the Divine Liturgy, the Lord's Supper, Holy Communion: Christians name it and understand it in genuinely different ways. But everyone is doing what Jesus did the night before he died. And one of its names is the everyday Greek way to say thank you.
screen: `A HOST LIFTED, A BELL RINGS.` → `A SPOON, TRAYS OF CUPS, A RAIL.` → `THE SAME NIGHT, REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Eucharist, from the Greek eucharistia: thanksgiving. Eu, good. Charis, grace, gift. In Greece today, efcharistó still means thank you. Paul passes on that night in a letter to Corinth, in the King James Bible: "And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me." Given thanks: that's the verb, eucharisteō. So what happens at that table? Churches differ, in earnest. Catholics believe the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood while still looking like bread and wine; they call this transubstantiation. Orthodox Christians also say Christ is truly present, and prefer to call it a holy mystery rather than explain how. Lutherans say Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. Many Reformed and Presbyterian Christians say Christ is truly present, but spiritually, received by faith. Many Baptists and others see a memorial, a powerful act of remembering, as Jesus said: do this in remembrance of me. Anglicans hold a range of these views within one church. How often varies too: daily Mass for some Catholics, weekly for many churches, monthly or quarterly for others. Under the disagreement sits something every one of these churches would say: this meal begins with gratitude. Before anything else, Jesus gave thanks.
screen: `EUCHARISTIA — THANKSGIVING.` · `WHEN HE HAD GIVEN THANKS, HE BRAKE IT.` · `TRULY PRESENT, SPIRITUAL, OR MEMORIAL.` · `IT BEGINS WITH GRATITUDE.` · then, large: `THIS DO IN REMEMBRANCE OF ME.`

segments.voice: This isn't communion, just an ordinary bite, eaten slowly: hold a piece of bread or a cracker, or imagine one, and think of the wheat, the field, the baker, the hands it passed through to reach you. Say thank you in whatever way you say it, then take one small bite and taste it. If you pray, give thanks to God; if you don't, give thanks to everyone who brought it to you.
Eucharist. Greek for thanksgiving. The Lord's Supper, named for the thanks Jesus gave before he broke the bread.
Your line: thanksgiving. In Greek, it's still how you say thank you. See you tomorrow.

154.title: Confession and anointing
154.hook: Catholics and Orthodox confess to a priest; Anglicans may; most Protestants confess to God directly or to a friend (James 5:16)
154.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess to a priest and receive absolution, and are anointed with oil when seriously ill; Anglicans may confess privately; most Protestants confess to God directly or to a trusted friend, and many churches anoint and pray for the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Eucharist, thanksgiving, the meal named for Jesus's thanks. Your line was thanksgiving.

A secret can sit in the chest like a stone. Something done, something said, something hidden. Days go by, and it gets heavier, not lighter. Then one evening it finally comes out, to a friend, a partner, a parent, in a shaky voice. It doesn't disappear. But often, it loosens. A short letter in the New Testament, from James, puts this in one plain sentence, right next to another practice: oil and prayer for the sick.
screen: `A STONE IN THE CHEST.` → `FINALLY, IT'S SAID.` → `IT LOOSENS.`

segments.voice: From James chapter five, in the King James Bible: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." Then: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." Oil for the sick, honest words for wrongs done. Start with confession. Catholics and Orthodox Christians confess their sins to a priest in a sacrament; Catholics call it reconciliation or penance. The priest speaks words of absolution, forgiveness in God's name, and he is bound never to reveal what he's heard. In many Orthodox churches, the person stands before an icon of Christ with the priest beside them, and the priest calls himself only a witness. Anglicans offer private confession too, with an old saying: all may, none must, some should. Most Protestants confess directly to God, and some also to a trusted friend or small group, taking James literally: one to another. A line from John's first letter is often said: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins." Now anointing. Catholics call it the anointing of the sick; it was once given mostly to the dying, and today it's for anyone seriously ill or facing surgery. Orthodox Christians call it holy unction, and in many churches everyone is anointed during Holy Week. Some Protestant churches, Pentecostal ones among them, anoint the sick and pray, as James describes. Words said out loud, oil on the skin: nobody should carry sickness or guilt alone.

Don't argue or explain; just name it plainly to yourself. If you pray, confess it to God in your own words, quietly or out loud, and sit with the promise of forgiveness; if you don't, say it to the silence and notice what happens to the weight.
Absolution, the priest's words of forgiveness spoken in God's name after confession, one of two practices James paired: honest words and healing oil.
